7:1.text: In those days, and at that time, will I cause the Branch of righteousness to grow up unto David; and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land.

provenance.other: “execute judgment” occurs in exactly 11 KJV verses, so the verb phrase alone points nowhere. What narrows it is the third term: “execute judgment and righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 33:15, and its twin at Jeremiah 23:5 supplies the only other member of the pair — “judgment and justice in the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ether 7:1 has all three of Jeremiah 33:15's elements: execute, judgment, righteousness, and the land.
provenance.alternative: Jeremiah 21:12's “Execute judgment in the” is also a KJV singleton, but it is an imperative addressed to the house of David about the oppressed, and nothing of its content appears here.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the formula is not a general commendation of good government but the sign of the Davidic Branch: 'I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.' The Book of Mormon's first Jaredite king — a gentile ruling a gentile people, on the text's own chronology some fifteen centuries before Jeremiah and outside the covenant entirely — is introduced in the King James English reserved for the messianic heir of David, and the sentence that follows him through the chapter (7:11, 7:27) is that same formula. Read metaleptically, the chapter is asserting that the office of the righteous king is not Israel's property: what Jeremiah promises to David, Ether reports as already having happened at Moron.

7:1.note: 'Orihah did execute judgement upon the land in righteousness all his days.' Three of the four content words of Jeremiah 33:15's closing clause, redistributed but intact — execute, judgement, righteousness, and the land. The redistribution is what keeps this at allusion rather than quotation: Jeremiah has 'execute judgment and righteousness in the land', Ether has 'execute judgement upon the land in righteousness', which is the same lexical stock through a different syntax and well short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold. The recurrence is the argument's real weight. The formula is not used once and dropped; it opens the chapter at 7:1, marks Shule's accession at 7:11, and closes the chapter at 7:27, so it functions as the chapter's evaluative refrain in the way 'he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD' functions in Kings — but the words chosen for it are Jeremiah's Branch oracle, not Kings'. CONVENTIONS §8 applies to the spelling: 1830 reads 'judgement' at all four occurrences and 1920 changed it to 'judgment', which is the KJV's own spelling, so the later edition moved the text toward its source rather than away.

7:2.text: And he had thirty sons that rode on thirty ass colts, and they had thirty cities, which are called Havothjair unto this day, which are in the land of Gilead.

provenance.other: “thirty sons” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 10:4 (Jair) and Judges 12:9 (Ibzan); Judges 12:14 gives Abdon forty. Judges 10:2 supplies the other numeral in play here — Tola 'judged Israel twenty and three years'. Every one of these verses is in the minor-judges notices, and nowhere else in the KJV is a ruler's entire biography a count of his years and a count of his children.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's account of Orihah gives him two facts and no others: he executed judgment all his days, and he begat a specified number of children of whom a specified number were sons. That is the form of the minor-judges notice and it is a form, not a phrase — which is why this is filed as figural. What the form imports is a theory of succession: in Judges the fertility notice is the whole of a good ruler's record because nothing happened in his time, and Ether 7 immediately falsifies that peace in the next two verses, when Corihor rebels. Orihah is given a judge's obituary and his sons give him a king's civil war.

7:2.note: 'Whose days were exceeding many. And he begat sons and daughters; yea, he begat thirty and one, among whom were twenty and three sons.' The candidate list offered Numbers 26:62 for 'twenty and three' — a Levite census total — and Genesis 5:4 for 'he begat sons and daughters', neither of which explains why a ruler's reign should be summarised by an offspring count at all. Judges does explain it: Jair had thirty sons and thirty cities, Ibzan thirty sons and thirty daughters, Abdon forty sons and thirty nephews, and Tola judged Israel twenty and three years, which is Ether's other numeral. Ether 7:1-2 reproduces the notice's two components in the notice's order — length of rule, then numbered offspring — and reproduces its silence about everything else.
7:2.whyNot: The only shared vocabulary is numerals, and numerals are the cheapest coincidence in a corpus that counts as compulsively as the KJV does. 'Thirty and one' and 'twenty and three' are not Judges' numbers; Judges has thirty, forty and seventy. A reader who wants nothing here but a common ancient way of praising a ruler's fruitfulness is not refuted by anything in this row, and the row would be withdrawn if it turned out that the Book of Mormon summarises other reigns this way — it does not; Orihah's is the only such notice in Ether.

7:3.text: For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.

provenance.other: “in his old age” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 21:2 and Genesis 21:7, and both are the birth of Isaac. The machine proposed Genesis 37:3, but its wording is “son of his old age”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is a different construction; “her old age” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:36, of Elisabeth. The English phrase Ether uses belongs, in the KJV, to Abraham alone.
provenance.significance: The KJV keeps this phrase for the promised son — the heir who arrives after the possibility has closed, 'at the set time of which God had spoken'. Ether 7 uses it three times, and the middle use is the one that matters: 7:7, 'nevertheless Kib begat Shule in his old age, while he was yet in captivity'. The deposed king, imprisoned by one son, fathers in prison the son who will free him. Reading the Isaac context back into it, the Jaredite deliverer is born under the Genesis sign of an impossible birth, and the 'nevertheless' in Ether's sentence is doing the work Genesis 21's 'set time' does — the succession is not broken because a son came when none could.

7:3.note: Adjudicated at its first occurrence, 7:3, though the argument is carried by 7:7 and the phrase returns a third time at 7:26 when Shule in turn begets in his old age. Three uses of a phrase the King James Bible reserves for Isaac's birth, in a chapter that is about nothing except whether a dynasty can survive its own sons, is more than the ordinary way to say a man was old. What holds the row at 'moderate' rather than higher is that the phrase is short and unremarkable in modern English, so a reader who takes it as plain description rather than borrowing has a case; the reply is that plain description is available in the KJV in half a dozen other forms ('well stricken in years', 'old and full of days') and this is the one that came.

7:3.text: And Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead.

provenance.other: “reigned in his stead” occurs in exactly 63 KJV verses, so no single verse can be named as the source and the row is filed on the formula rather than on a citation. Of those 63, the first seven are Genesis 36:33-39, and they are the only place in the KJV where the formula runs as an unbroken chain outside the regnal histories of Israel and Judah.
provenance.significance: Genesis 36:31 heads that chain: 'these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel.' It is the King James Bible's one gentile king-list, kept precisely because it is prior to and outside Israel's monarchy, and it is exactly the thing the book of Ether claims to be. Ether 7 does not borrow a verse from it; it borrows the genre, down to the formula that stitches the generations together. Reading the two lists against each other is the interesting result: Genesis 36 records a gentile succession with no evaluation at all, and Ether 7 takes the same form and inserts into it prophets, idolatry, repentance and a curse upon the land — the Deuteronomic machinery that Genesis 36 conspicuously withholds from Edom.

7:3.note: 'And it came to pass that Kib reigned in his stead.' The formula recurs at 7:10 ('he began to reign in the stead of his father') and at 7:19 ('did build up his kingdom in his stead'), and it is the connective tissue of the whole Jaredite record. Filed as figural rather than allusion because 63 KJV verses cannot be narrowed to one, and no argument here rests on the reader recovering a particular Edomite king. What the row records is that the Book of Mormon's dynastic book is written in the KJV's dynastic English, and that the KJV's model for a dynastic list belonging to a people outside Israel is Genesis 36.
7:3.whyNot: A formula occurring in 63 verses is close to the boundary CONVENTIONS §5 draws around connective noise, and an adjudicator who filed this as a standing exclusion rather than a link would be applying the rules correctly. The row is written instead because the formula is not connective — it is generic, it marks a genre, and a reader of Ether who is shown nothing at all here has been told there is no borrowing in the Book of Mormon's most conspicuously biblical sentence pattern. Withdraw it if a better-evidenced link to the Kings regnal formula is made at an earlier Jaredite accession, which would displace Genesis 36 as the model.

7:4.text: After this man rose up Judas of Galilee in the days of the taxing, and drew away much people after him: he also perished; and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed.

provenance.other: “drew away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:37, and the clause the Book of Mormon writes is that verse's clause with one word changed: 'drew away much people after him' becomes 'drew away many people after him'. Six words, five of them identical and all six in order, on a phrase the King James Bible uses once.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:37 is not narrative but evidence in an argument. Gamaliel cites Theudas and Judas of Galilee to the council as the two cases proving his rule: a movement that is of men comes to nought of itself, so leave the apostles alone. The King James Bible's only man who 'drew away' a people after him is therefore its type-specimen of the insurrection that fails. Ether 7 gives the sentence to Corihor and then declines Gamaliel's conclusion twice over — Corihor's rising does not come to nought, it succeeds, deposes the king and holds him in captivity for a generation; and Corihor himself does not perish with his followers dispersed but 'repented of the many evils which he had done' and is given power in his brother's kingdom (7:13). The borrowed clause carries Gamaliel's rule into the chapter and the chapter breaks it.

7:4.note: 'Wherefore Corihor drew away many people after him.' The strongest row in the chapter and the one the candidate list missed entirely — the n-gram stream ranked Judges 6:33 and Matthew 10:35 at this verse and never proposed Acts 5. The evidence is as clean as this catalogue gets: a six-word clause reproduced with a single substitution from a phrase that occurs once in the KJV, in a source whose subject is precisely a man who draws a people away after himself. It falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six, but by the standard set at 1 Nephi 1:14 — six exact words from a two-verse rarity, catalogued as quotation — the volume here is greater, not less. The construction is the chapter's, not a single verse's accident: Shule arms 'those which he had drew away with him' at 7:9, and Noah 'drew away Cohor his brother' at 7:15. CONVENTIONS §8 bears on the middle one: the 1830 reads 'he had drew away', which is ungrammatical and was corrected to 'drawn' in 1920, so the first edition preserves the verb in a form no KJV verse has while keeping the KJV's phrase.

7:4.text: Jehoram was thirty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “thirty and two years old” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 2 Kings 8:17, 2 Chronicles 21:5 and 2 Chronicles 21:20, and all three are the same man: Jehoram of Judah, whose age at accession the KJV records three times and no other king's at thirty-two.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 21:4, the verse immediately before, is what makes the number worth a row: 'Now when Jehoram was risen up to the kingdom of his father, he strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword.' The KJV's one thirty-two-year-old is the king who takes his father's kingdom and destroys his own brothers to hold it, and Ether 7:4 gives that age to the son who rebels against his father and whose brother must later take the kingdom back from him by battle. Neither text mentions the other; the number is doing the work of a marginal cross-reference.

7:4.note: 'And when Corihor was thirty and two years old, he rebelled against his father.' The machine ranked 2 Chronicles 21:5 here for the run 'thirty and two years old', and the ordinary verdict on a regnal numeral is the one the register gives at Helaman 1:1 — the KJV counts constantly and a shared number is arithmetic, not borrowing. What makes this one different is that the number is not distributed: all three of its KJV occurrences are one king, and that king's defining act is fratricidal usurpation within the father's house, which is the act Ether 7:4 is narrating. Filed as an echo, at moderate, because the verbal contact is a number and nothing else.
7:4.whyNot: A number is the weakest possible carrier of dependence and the Book of Mormon supplies ages and reign-lengths continually without biblical parallel. Ether 7:4 uses the number for age at rebellion, not age at accession, so even the syntactic frame differs from all three KJV verses. If a reader holds that the coincidence is one in a few dozen and that the chapter's real Jehoram-shaped material is elsewhere, this row does not survive; it is recorded so that a reader who notices the singleton king is told the catalogue noticed too.

7:5.text: So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

provenance.other: “brought to pass the saying” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does the shorter “to pass the saying”. The KJV has many formulas for fulfilment — 'that it might be fulfilled', 'the word of the LORD came to pass' — and this is not one of the common ones; it is Paul's, once.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 15:54 is itself quoting Isaiah 25:8, so this is a mediation case and tools/mediation-check.py was run on Ether 7:5 against both. It is decisive for the New Testament: the Book of Mormon has 1 Corinthians 15:54's frame ('brought to pass the saying') and not one word of Isaiah 25:8, whose 'He will swallow up death in victory' supplies the content Paul quotes and nothing the Book of Mormon uses. What is borrowed here is the wrapper, not what is inside it.
provenance.significance: This is metalepsis of an unusually exact kind, because the borrowed frame is a slot with a fixed filler. In the King James Bible the one 'saying' that is 'brought to pass' is 'Death is swallowed up in victory' — the abolition of death at the resurrection, the climax of Paul's argument. Ether 7:5 keeps the frame and substitutes the filler: the saying brought to pass is the brother of Jared's, 'That they would be brought into captivity.' Recover the context and the sentence is doing the opposite of what its source does. Paul's formula announces the end of bondage; Ether's announces the beginning of one, and it does so in the first generation of a people who were promised a land of liberty.

7:5.note: 'Which brought to pass the saying of the brother of Jared, That they would be brought into captivity.' Five consecutive words on a KJV singleton, and the machine ranked it first at this verse for exactly that reason — one of the few places in the chapter where the n-gram stream was right. The row is 'allusion' rather than 'quotation' because what is reproduced is a citation formula and not a proposition: the Book of Mormon is not repeating Paul's saying, it is using Paul's sentence for introducing one. Confidence is 'high' rather than 'certain' on the ground that fulfilment formulas are the kind of language a writer might reconstruct from general familiarity with the KJV without any one verse in view — but the KJV offers a dozen other fulfilment formulas that are far commoner, and this is the rare one.

7:17.text: Then they took the king, and carried him up unto the king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; where he gave judgment upon him.

provenance.other: “took the king and carried” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The second half of Ether's clause comes from the same deportation vocabulary: “away captive into”, with a place-name following, occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 39:9 and Luke 21:24. tools/mediation-check.py on Ether 7:17 against those two is decisive for Jeremiah — the Book of Mormon has 'carried … away captive into' where Luke has 'led away captive into'.
provenance.alternative: “carried him away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 15:1 — 'bound Jesus, and carried him away, and delivered him to Pilate' — and the sequence there is the same one Ether has: a king is seized, carried away, and about to be put to death. It is filed in the exclusion register at this verse rather than as a composite, because Jeremiah 52:9 accounts for the whole clause and Mark 15:1 accounts only for three words of it.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 52 is the fall of Jerusalem, and the king taken and carried away is Zedekiah, in whose reign 1 Nephi opens. The Book of Mormon's other deportation sentence, at 1 Nephi 1:13, is the prophecy that Jerusalem should be destroyed 'and many should be carried away captive into Babylon' — the catalogue's flagship rarity. Ether 7:17 writes the fulfilled form of that same sentence for a king in a different hemisphere fifteen centuries earlier, substituting Moron for Babylon. What follows is the point of the substitution. Jeremiah 52:10-11 has Zedekiah's sons slain before his eyes and the king himself kept in prison till the day of his death; Ether 7:18 has the sons of Shule break down the door of the prison and set their father back on his throne. The Jaredite record takes the KJV's worst royal ending and reverses the role of the sons in it.

7:17.note: 'And he took Shule the king, and carried him away captive into Moron.' The candidate list gave Jeremiah 52:9 for 'took the king and carried' and Mark 15:1 for 'carried him away', and reading the whole verse decides between them: Ether's clause has the object ('the king'), the verb pair ('took … and carried'), the qualifier ('captive') and a named destination, which is Jeremiah's shape entire and Mark's only in part. Set beside 1 Nephi 1:13 this is the same idiom in a different hand and a different book, so CONVENTIONS §4's across-a-book-boundary rule applies: the row is written in full here rather than deferred to its first adjudication, and recurrenceRefs sends the reader back to it.

7:22.text: And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.

provenance.other: “Nimrod” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Genesis 10:8, Genesis 10:9, 1 Chronicles 1:10 and Micah 5:6. Of those, Genesis 10:10 is the verse that attaches a kingdom to him, and it is the verse immediately following the two that name him. kjvSpecific is 'no' because a proper name is spelled the same in every English Bible and there is no wording here to test — the rarity is the name itself, not the KJV's rendering of it.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has already been to Genesis 10 in this book: at Ether 2:1 the Jaredites cross 'the valley of Nimrod, being called after the mighty hunter', which lifts a KJV singleton and is catalogued there as certain. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 10:8-9 at that verse. What 7:22 adds is the second half of the Genesis notice. Genesis 10:10 says 'the beginning of his kingdom was Babel' — Nimrod is the KJV's first empire-builder, and the tower his kingdom begins with is the tower whose confounding, at Genesis 11, is the founding event of the entire Jaredite record (Ether 1:33). Ether 7:22 then gives the name to a prince who does the one thing the Genesis Nimrod is incapable of: 'Nimrod gave up the kingdom of Cohor unto Shule.' The man whose name means the beginning of a kingdom surrenders one. It is hard to read that as accident in a book that opens at Babel.

7:22.note: 'And now Cohor had a son which was called Nimrod.' A name and not a phrase, which is why the row is conceptual and why kjvSpecific is 'no'; but a name that occurs four times in the King James Bible, three of them in one genealogy, and which arrives here in a book whose premise is that genealogy's next chapter. The row is written rather than passed over because Ether has demonstrably used Genesis 10 already, at 2:1, where the borrowing is a KJV singleton and the confidence is certain — availability of the source is not in question within this book, only the significance of a second visit. Per CONVENTIONS §4 this is not a narrator reusing his own formula: 2:1 borrows Nimrod's title for a place, 7:22 borrows his name for a person, and the second use argues something the first does not, because the thing this Nimrod does with a kingdom is the reverse of what Genesis 10:10 records of his namesake.

7:24.text: Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.

provenance.route: Matthew 5:11-12 and 2 Chronicles 36:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “revile” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 22:28 and Matthew 5:11; Ether 7:24 uses it twice. Matthew 5:11-12 is the only place in the King James Bible where reviling and prophets stand together — 'when men shall revile you … for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you'. The other verb is the Old Testament's: “mocked the messengers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “misused his prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both 2 Chronicles 36:16, which is also the only KJV verse in which mocking and prophets stand together.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py was run on Ether 7:24 against 2 Chronicles 36:16 and Matthew 5:11 and reports divergences pointing both ways, one decisive point for each — which is the honest result here, not a failure of the tool. Ether 7:24 has the New Testament's rare verb ('revile', twice) applied to the Old Testament's object ('the prophets'), so it is a fusion of the KJV's two treatments of the theme rather than a following of either. Mediation is recorded as 'direct-NT' because the source verse named is Matthew 5:11 and no earlier Book of Mormon passage is the proximate model; the Chronicles half of the fusion is carried in `composite` and argued here.
provenance.significance: Both sources come with an outcome attached and Ether 7 takes neither. 2 Chronicles 36:16 is the epitaph of Judah: they mocked and misused the prophets 'until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy', and the next verse is the Chaldeans. Matthew 5:12 tells the disciples to rejoice at the same treatment because it is what the prophets always got. Ether 7:24-26 supplies the remedy that Chronicles says did not exist — the king prosecutes the mockers, legislates the prophets' freedom of movement, and 'the people were brought unto repentance' — and in doing so removes the occasion for the beatitude, since in Shule's kingdom reviling a prophet is a crime rather than a blessing. Note also what this does beside 1 Nephi 1: Lehi is mocked at Jerusalem and must flee, which is Chronicles' outcome; Shule's Jaredites are the counterfactual.

7:24.note: 'The people did revile against the prophets, and did mock them … king Shule did execute judgement against all those who did revile against the prophets.' The candidate list proposed nothing at this verse, which is a good illustration of CONVENTIONS §9 — the agreement is lexical and split across a clause boundary, exactly what a contiguous n-gram window cannot see. What is there is two rare verbs, each of which the KJV attaches to prophets in exactly one place, arriving in the same sentence. Held at 'moderate' because neither source supplies a clause and the shared material is two words; what carries it above 'low' is that the two words are not synonyms drawn at random from a wide field, but the King James Bible's only two ways of saying what men do to prophets.

7:27.text: And there was no more war unto the five and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa.

provenance.other: “no more war” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 15:19. Judges' recurring peace formula is 'the land had rest', which “had rest” shows in exactly 8 KJV verses and which the Book of Mormon does not use here.
provenance.significance: The singleton is the tail of a sequence, and it is the sequence Ether 7:23-27 runs in order. 2 Chronicles 15: a prophet is sent to the king (15:1-7); the king takes courage and 'put away the abominable idols out of all the land' (15:8, itself a KJV singleton); the people enter a covenant to seek the LORD (15:12); they are spared and given rest (15:15); 'and there was no more war' (15:19). Ether 7: 'there came prophets among the people, which were sent from the Lord' about the people's 'wickedness and idolatry' (7:23); the king executes judgment on those who revile them and passes a law protecting them (7:24-25); 'because the people did repent of their iniquities and idolatries, the Lord did spare them, and they began to prosper again in the land' (7:26); 'and there was no more wars in the days of Shule' (7:27). Five stages, same order, closing on the KJV's one occurrence of the closing phrase. Read the other way, the metalepsis cuts: Asa's rest expires at a stated year — 'unto the five and thirtieth year' — and 2 Chronicles 16 has Asa turn on a seer and imprison him. Ether's phrase is bounded by 'in the days of Shule', which does the same work; the peace is dated, and the next chapter is Ether 8's secret combinations.

7:27.note: 'And there was no more wars in the days of Shule.' A four-word run on a KJV singleton would be a modest row on its own; what makes it a strong one is that the singleton sits at the end of the only reform narrative in the King James Bible with the same five stages in the same order, and the Book of Mormon has just run all five. The verbal contact and the structural contact are pointing at the same chapter, which is the shape ADJUDICATING §3 asks for. CONVENTIONS §8 applies to the grammar: 1830 reads 'there was no more wars' and 1920 corrected it to 'were'. The 1830's singular verb is what the KJV has ('there was no more war'), with the noun pluralised — so the first edition is closer to its source than the current text is, and the 1920 correction moved the sentence away from Chronicles by tidying it.

7:27.text: And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great works of the LORD, that he did for Israel.

provenance.other: “great works of the LORD” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 2:7, and “seen all the great” occurs in exactly two, Judges 2:7 and Deuteronomy 11:7. The Book of Mormon's noun is 'things' rather than 'works', and the four-word run it does reproduce, “the Lord had done for”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 1 Kings 8:66, at the dedication of the temple. The clause here is therefore Judges 2:7's thought in 1 Kings 8:66's words.
provenance.significance: Judges 2:7-10 is the KJV's statement of how a nation forgets: the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who had seen what he did, 'and there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel.' Ether 7:27 is the first half of that, exactly — a ruler characterised by remembering a deliverance he did not witness, and the peace lasting his days and being bounded by them. The second half is Ether 8, which opens on Shule's grandson and the secret combinations. The Book of Mormon has put a Judges 2:7 sentence at the last verse of the chapter and then supplied Judges 2:10.

7:27.note: 'He remembered the great things that the Lord had done for his fathers in bringing them across the great deep into the promised land.' The candidate list offered 1 Kings 8:66 and 2 Kings 8:4 for the run, and 2 Kings 8:4 is the wrong one: 'the great things that Elisha hath done' is Gehazi entertaining a king with prophet stories, with no deliverance and no fathers. 1 Kings 8:66 supplies the exact four-word run but is a crowd going home cheerful after a festival. Judges 2:7 supplies what the Book of Mormon verse actually is — the formula for a generation that keeps faith because it remembers a founding deliverance, framed by 'all the days' of the leader who remembers, which is Ether 7:27's own frame ('all his days'). Held at 'moderate': the closest wording and the closest sense are in two different verses, and a row that has to take one from each is weaker than one that takes both from the same place.
